title: Files & Object Storage
subtitle: Follow a 2 GB video upload straight into an object store, and see why your API server never touches the bytes.
learn: How block, file, and object storage differ and which fits which job
Why big files go in an object store and their metadata in a database
How a presigned URL lets a client upload without passing through your API
How multipart upload makes huge uploads resumable and parallel
How a CDN serves reads and how an upload event triggers background work

steps.title: Where do the bytes go?
steps.body: A user taps Upload on a 2 GB video. Your app also needs to remember who owns it, its title, and whether it has been processed. Do you push 2 GB through your API servers into a database column? Almost nobody does. This lesson shows where the bytes live, where the facts about them live, and how they travel between the two.
steps.idea: Big binary data and small structured facts want different homes.
steps.caption: A client holds a large file; the system must store it safely.

steps.title: Block, file, object
steps.body: Block storage is a raw disk: fixed-size blocks you read and write at an offset, ideal for a database's data files or a VM disk. File storage adds folders and paths on top and lets many machines share them (NFS-style). Object storage, like S3, is a flat bucket of whole objects found by key: you PUT or GET the entire thing, and you cannot edit bytes in the middle on classic S3-style stores (you replace the whole object). In exchange you get huge scale, cheap cost per GB, and very high durability (S3 advertises 11 nines).
steps.idea: Block is for databases and VMs, file is for shared folders, object is for blobs at scale.
steps.caption: The object store holds whole, immutable blobs addressed by key.

steps.title: The naive path: proxy it
steps.body: The simplest design: client sends the file to the API, and the API forwards it to the object store. It works, but now every upload ties up an API connection for the whole transfer. Ten thousand users each uploading 2 GB means your API fleet moves 20 TB, and each byte crosses your API fleet's network twice (in from the client, out to the store). A slow phone on bad Wi-Fi holds a worker for minutes.
steps.idea: Proxying uploads makes your API a bandwidth pipe, which is the wrong thing to scale.
steps.caption: Every byte passes through the API server twice.

steps.title: Metadata DB + blob
steps.body: Split the job. The blob lives in the object store under a key such as videos/u42/9f3a.mp4. A row in the metadata database records the facts: owner, title, size, content type, the object key, and a status like pending. The database answers questions like list my videos by date, which an object store cannot do well (it only lists keys by prefix). The row is the index; the blob is the payload.
steps.idea: Store the key and facts in a database; store the bytes in the object store.
steps.caption: Client asks to upload; API records a pending row.

steps.title: Presigned URL
steps.body: The API now asks its storage library to sign a URL for exactly one operation: PUT this key, valid for 15 minutes. Signing is local math with a secret the client never sees, so it costs microseconds and no storage call. The client receives the URL and can upload to the store directly. For a small file, one signed PUT URL is enough; for big files see the next step. Anyone holding the URL can use it until it expires, so keep lifetimes short and scope it to one key.
steps.idea: A presigned URL is a short-lived permission slip: the API grants it, the store honors it.
steps.caption: API hands the client a signed, expiring upload URL.

steps.title: Upload in parts
steps.body: A single 2 GB PUT is fragile: if the connection drops at 95 percent, you start over. For a big file the API starts a multipart upload, then signs one URL per part (here 32 parts of 64 MB; S3 needs 5 MiB or more per part except the last). The client PUTs the parts straight to the store, in parallel, and collects an ETag for each. Then it sends the ETag list to the API, which calls complete and the store stitches the parts into one object. A failed part is retried alone.
steps.idea: Multipart makes big uploads parallel and resumable: retry a part, not the file.
steps.caption: API signs 32 part URLs; client uploads parts straight to the store.

steps.title: React to the upload
steps.body: When the object appears, the store emits an event (for example ObjectCreated) onto a queue. A worker picks it up and treats the upload as untrusted: it checks type and size, generates thumbnails or transcodes, then flips the row from pending to ready. If the worker crashes, the message is redelivered. Delivery is at-least-once, so processing must be safe to run twice. S3 reads of new objects are strongly consistent, so the worker sees the file right away.
steps.idea: Use storage events to trigger background work and flip the row to ready.
steps.caption: Object arrives, event fires, worker marks the row ready.

steps.title: Serve it from the edge
steps.body: To watch the video, the client asks the API where it is (a metadata DB lookup) and gets a CDN URL. Public content goes through the CDN: the first viewer in a region causes a cache miss and the CDN pulls from the object store, and later viewers get the cached copy from nearby. Private files use a presigned GET URL straight from the store, or CDN-signed URLs if you still want edge caching.
steps.idea: Read through a CDN for speed and cost; use presigned GET for private files.
steps.caption: CDN fills from the store on a miss, then serves nearby.

steps.title: The upload is abandoned
steps.body: The user closes the app after 20 of 32 parts. Those parts sit in the store, invisible but billed, and the row is stuck on pending. Two cleanups fix this: a lifecycle rule that aborts incomplete multipart uploads after, say, 7 days, and a job that deletes pending rows older than a day and aborts their multipart upload. The mirror problem is deleting a row but forgetting the blob, so deletes should remove both.
steps.idea: Two systems mean two cleanups: expire stale multipart parts and stale pending rows.
steps.caption: A dropped upload leaves orphaned parts behind.

steps.title: The whole pattern
steps.body: Bytes go in an object store, facts go in a metadata database, and the API only brokers permission. A presigned URL lets the client upload directly, multipart makes huge files resumable, events trigger processing, and a CDN serves reads. Block storage stays for databases and VM disks. Object stores cannot edit in place, so changing a file means writing a new object.
steps.idea: Keep your API out of the data path: sign a URL, let the client talk to the store.
steps.caption: API handles tiny messages; the store handles gigabytes.

quiz.q: Why do most designs hand the client a presigned URL instead of proxying the upload through the API?
options: Object stores refuse requests that come from API servers
Presigned URLs encrypt the file, and the API cannot
The file bytes skip your API, so it only handles a tiny request and scales independently of upload volume
It removes the need for a metadata database
quiz.why: The signature is created locally and the client sends bytes directly to the store, so API servers do not carry upload bandwidth. You still need a database for metadata.

quiz.q: A 2 GB multipart upload of 32 parts fails on part 27 because of a network blip. What should the client do?
options: Retry only part 27, then complete the upload
Delete the metadata row and ask the user to try again later
quiz.why: Each part is uploaded and acknowledged independently with its own ETag, so only the failed part needs to be resent before the complete call.

quiz.q: Why store the object key and attributes in a database row rather than relying on the bucket alone?
options: Buckets cannot hold more than 1 million objects
Object keys cannot contain the user's name
Objects are encrypted so they cannot be read back
The database can query by owner, date or status, while a bucket mainly lists keys by prefix
quiz.why: Object stores are good at get-by-key and prefix listing. Questions like all videos owned by user 42 this week belong in a database that can index those fields.

quiz.q: You need to update a single 4 KB page in the middle of a large data file many times per second. Which storage fits best?
options: Object storage, rewriting the object each time
Block storage, which supports reads and writes at an offset
A CDN with a short TTL
A presigned URL with a long lifetime
quiz.why: Block storage allows small in-place writes at an offset, which is why databases use it. Objects are replaced whole, so a 4 KB edit would mean rewriting the entire object.

cheatsheet.def: Raw fixed-size blocks read or written at an offset. Used for database files and VM disks. Low latency, in-place updates.
Hierarchical folders and paths, often shared by many machines over a network. Good for shared home directories and legacy apps.
Flat bucket of whole objects found by key. Cheap, huge, durable, but no partial edits: replace the whole object.
Keep owner, size, status and the object key in a database row; keep the bytes in the object store. The row is how you search and list.
A time-limited URL signed by your server for one operation on one key. Lets a client talk directly to the store. Keep expiry short.

Split a large file into parts (S3: 5 MiB to 5 GiB each, max 10,000). The API starts the upload and signs one URL per part; the client uploads in parallel, retries failed parts, then the API completes. Abort stale ones with a lifecycle rule.
The store emits a notification when an object is created, so a worker can scan, resize or transcode it. Handlers must be idempotent.
Cache popular objects at edge locations. Cuts latency and egress cost; for private content use a presigned GET from the store, or CDN-signed URLs to keep edge caching.
